# 1.1 The Rise of Authoritarian States and the Causes of World War II

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why authoritarianism rose

**Economic despair caused by the Great Depression led people to seek alternatives to liberal democracy, which seemed to have failed.** That sentence is the core of the topic — the appeal of authoritarian movements is inseparable from the economic collapse of 1929.

**Germany.** The **Treaty of Versailles (1919)** punished Germany severely: loss of territory, military restrictions, and heavy reparations. **National humiliation combined with economic collapse** made the German public receptive to Hitler's message of restoring German pride.

**Italy.** **Economic stagnation and fear of socialism** helped Mussolini rise by presenting fascism as a **"third way"** between capitalism and communism.

**Japan.** **Economic instability** and a desire for resources gave **military leaders** influence, and they promoted **expansion as the solution** — invading **Manchuria in 1931**.

## Long-term causes of the war

| Cause | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Treaty of Versailles (1919)** | Harsh reparations and territorial losses created lasting resentment |
| **Failure of the League of Nations** | Could not prevent aggression in **Manchuria (1931)**, **Ethiopia (1935)**, or by Germany |
| **Rise of totalitarian regimes** | Fascism in Italy (Mussolini), Nazism in Germany (Hitler), militarism in Japan |
| **The Great Depression (1929)** | Enabled authoritarian parties to gain support by promising stability |
| **Expansionism** | Japan sought empire in Asia, Italy in Africa, Germany in Europe |
| **Anti-Comintern Pact (1936)** | Alliance between Germany and Japan against communism |

**Anti-communist sentiment** was itself a cause, since it allowed fascist nations to make common cause and made Western democracies reluctant to ally with the USSR.

## Appeasement

Western democracies — particularly **Britain and France** — pursued **appeasement**, allowing aggressive expansion in the hope of avoiding war:

- **Anschluss (1938)** — the annexation of Austria
- **The Sudetenland**, conceded at the **Munich Agreement (1938)**
- **March 1939** — Hitler took the rest of **Czechoslovakia**, demonstrating that the Munich promises were worthless

Earlier acts of aggression had already gone unanswered: **Japan's full invasion of China in 1937** and Italy's invasion of Ethiopia.

Appeasement is best understood in context rather than dismissed. The memory of the First World War was twenty years old, Britain and France were unprepared to fight, and the reasoning was that Germany's grievances over Versailles were partly legitimate. The judgement against it is that each concession strengthened Germany and confirmed that force worked.

## Immediate causes and outbreak

**The Nazi-Soviet Pact (Molotov-Ribbentrop, August 1939).** Germany and the USSR agreed not to attack each other, and **secretly agreed to divide Poland and Eastern Europe**. This removed Hitler's fear of a two-front war and made the invasion possible.

**Invasion of Poland (1 September 1939).** Germany attacked from the west using **blitzkrieg** — "lightning war", defeating opponents through a series of short, fast campaigns combining tanks, aircraft, and radio coordination. The **USSR invaded from the east on 17 September**.

Germany had **panzers** and a well-trained army, built up secretly over the preceding years in violation of Versailles.

**Britain and France declared war on 3 September 1939**, having recognised that appeasement had failed.

## The American position

The United States entered the war late for two reasons: the **Great Depression**, which brought severe economic damage and political instability, and the **trauma of the First World War**. President **Harding** had refused to join the League, arguing that America needed a **"return to normalcy"**, and the country remained in **isolationism** and formal **neutrality** through the 1930s. The isolationist position was popular, not merely governmental — which is why it took **Pearl Harbor** to end it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Treaty of Versailles (1919)** | The settlement that punished Germany severely with loss of territory, military restrictions, and heavy reparations; the harsh reparations and territorial losses created lasting resentment |
| **Expansionism** | Japan sought empire in Asia, Italy in Africa, Germany in Europe |
| **"Third way"** | Fascism as Mussolini presented it — an alternative between capitalism and communism |
| **Anti-Comintern Pact (1936)** | Alliance between Germany and Japan against communism |
| **Appeasement** | Allowing aggressive expansion in the hope of avoiding war, as Britain and France did |
| **Anschluss (1938)** | The annexation of Austria |
| **Munich Agreement (1938)** | The agreement at which the Sudetenland was conceded to Germany |
| **Nazi-Soviet Pact (Molotov-Ribbentrop, August 1939)** | Germany and the USSR agreed not to attack each other, and secretly agreed to divide Poland and Eastern Europe |
| **Blitzkrieg** | "Lightning war" — defeating opponents through a series of short, fast campaigns combining tanks, aircraft, and radio coordination |

# 2.1 World War II: Theatres and Key Battles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The European theatre

**Western Europe.** The **fall of France (June 1940)**, the **Dunkirk evacuation**, and the **Battle of Britain (1940)** — in which radar and the RAF prevented a German invasion.

**Eastern Front.** **Operation Barbarossa (1941)**, the German invasion of the USSR; the **Siege of Leningrad (1941–44)**; the **Battle of Moscow (1941)**; the **Battle of Stalingrad (1942–43)**; and the **Battle of Kursk (1943)**.

The Eastern Front is where most of the war's fighting and dying occurred. Germany's initial advance was successful, but the **Red Army** — the largest in the world, backed by vast natural resources — made a major comeback. Stalingrad is the turning point of the European war.

**North Africa.** The **Battle of El Alamein (1942)**, **Operation Torch (1942)**, and the **Axis surrender in Tunisia (1943)**.

### Operation Torch (November 1942)

The original plan was for Generals **George Marshall** and **Dwight Eisenhower** to invade German-occupied France directly, to draw German troops away from the USSR. That was judged premature, and the invasion of **North Africa** was substituted.

### The Casablanca Conference (January 1943)

Held in Casablanca in northwestern Morocco, where **Roosevelt and Churchill** met to decide the next steps — and agreed on **unconditional surrender** as the war's aim.

### The Italian campaign

The invasion of **Sicily (1943)**, then the mainland from the "toe" of Italy. The German commander's key strategy was the **Gustav Line** — a defensive entanglement of machine guns, booby traps, and mines built into Italy's mountainous terrain, which made the Italian campaign far slower and costlier than expected.

### The air war

Allied bombing targeted **production centres** and nearly annihilated the **Luftwaffe**, which was a precondition for D-Day: an amphibious landing is impossible without control of the air.

### D-Day (6 June 1944)

**Operation Overlord**, the **invasion of Normandy**, was the **largest amphibious operation of the war**, opening the Western Front and beginning the liberation of France.

**Why it succeeded:** the Allies **invaded by surprise**, landing at **Normandy rather than Calais**, where German forces expected them. Deception operations kept German reserves waiting in the wrong place for weeks.

**The Red Ball Express** supplied the advancing armies: designated routes were marked with **red balls**, and the trucks carried red-ball markings, so that other traffic could clear the roads for them.

### The Battle of the Bulge (1944)

The **last German counteroffensive**. Allied attempts to break into the heart of Germany met heavy losses for small gains — *"the wrong time, the wrong place"*, against a well-equipped German defence.

### The end in Europe

The Allies held that **the only solution was Germany's unconditional surrender**. The **Berlin Offensive (April–May 1945)** ended the fighting, and the European theatre officially closed on **2 May 1945**. **VE Day** was **8 May 1945**.

## The Pacific theatre

**Pearl Harbor (December 1941)** severely crippled the US Pacific fleet. Japan aimed to destroy American naval power in a single blow. Because the **battleship fleet** was crippled in Hawaii, the US had to fight with **aircraft carriers and submarines** — which, as it turned out, were the decisive weapons of the Pacific war. The attack thus forced the US into the naval doctrine that beat Japan.

**Key battles:** the **Battle of Midway (1942)**, **Guadalcanal (1942–43)**, and the **island-hopping campaign** — bypassing strongly held islands to seize those needed as airbases.

### Iwo Jima and Okinawa (February–April 1945)

**Iwo Jima** was a strategic air base between the Mariana Islands and Japan. Japanese preparations had **carved underground fortifications** turning the volcanic island into a defensive network, which is why the fighting was so costly.

**Okinawa** began on **1 April 1945**, the last invasion before the Japanese mainland. **Kamikaze** pilots deliberately crashed their aircraft into US carriers and battleships.

The ferocity of both battles fed directly into the decision described below: American planners projected casualties for an invasion of Japan by extrapolating from Okinawa.

### The end in the Pacific

In May 1945 the Allies remained sceptical, since Japan had not surrendered and might attack again. The **Manhattan Project** — the secret US programme to develop atomic weapons — produced the bombs dropped on **Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945**, the first use of nuclear weapons in warfare.

The Pacific theatre officially ended on **2 September**, the day the formal surrender documents were signed aboard the **USS Missouri** — which is why the official celebration came later than the news.

## The home fronts

**Total war** meant civilian economies fully mobilised: rationing, women entering the workforce, and propaganda.

| Country | Home front |
|---|---|
| **United States** | War Production Board; **internment of Japanese Americans** under Executive Order 9066; "Rosie the Riveter" |
| **Britain** | The Blitz; evacuation of children; radar; a war economy |
| **USSR** | Scorched earth; **relocation of industry east of the Urals** |
| **Germany** | Forced labour, Hitler Youth, propaganda under Goebbels |
| **Japan** | Mobilisation under state Shinto; kamikaze; anti-Western sentiment |

## Technology, intelligence, and science

- **Enigma and Ultra** — the British cracking of German codes. The Enigma machine could encode a single letter in an enormous number of ways, and breaking it shortened the war
- **Radar and sonar** — critical in the Battle of Britain and the Battle of the Atlantic
- **V-weapons** — German V-1 and V-2 rockets
- **Medical advances** — mass production of **penicillin**, and blood transfusion
- **Aircraft carriers** revolutionised naval warfare

## Scale

Estimates put total deaths at **60–85 million**, including military and civilian; roughly **40 million were civilians**. Germany's armed forces peaked at around 11 million.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battle of Britain (1940)** | The battle in which radar and the RAF prevented a German invasion |
| **Operation Barbarossa (1941)** | The German invasion of the USSR |
| **Red Army** | The Soviet army — the largest in the world, backed by vast natural resources |
| **Operation Torch (1942)** | The invasion of North Africa, substituted for the original plan of invading German-occupied France directly to draw German troops away from the USSR |
| **Casablanca Conference (January 1943)** | The meeting in northwestern Morocco where Roosevelt and Churchill decided the next steps and agreed on unconditional surrender as the war's aim |
| **Gustav Line** | The German commander's defensive entanglement of machine guns, booby traps, and mines built into Italy's mountainous terrain |
| **Operation Overlord (D-Day, 6 June 1944)** | The invasion of Normandy, the largest amphibious operation of the war, opening the Western Front and beginning the liberation of France |
| **Red Ball Express** | The supply operation for the advancing armies: designated routes were marked with red balls, and the trucks carried red-ball markings, so other traffic could clear the roads for them |
| **Battle of the Bulge (1944)** | The last German counteroffensive |
| **VE Day** | 8 May 1945; the European theatre had officially closed on 2 May 1945 |
| **Island-hopping campaign** | Bypassing strongly held islands to seize those needed as airbases |
| **Iwo Jima** | A strategic air base between the Mariana Islands and Japan, where Japanese preparations had carved underground fortifications turning the volcanic island into a defensive network |
| **Kamikaze** | Pilots who deliberately crashed their aircraft into US carriers and battleships |
| **Manhattan Project** | The secret US programme to develop atomic weapons |

| **V-weapons** | German V-1 and V-2 rockets |

# 3.1 The Holocaust

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

The **Holocaust** was the **systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews** by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, between **1933 and 1945**. The Hebrew term is **the Shoah**, meaning catastrophe.

Millions of others were also murdered: **Roma**, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners of war, and others.

## Antisemitism

The primary target was **Jews**, and the ideology behind it was **antisemitism** — prejudice against or hatred of Jewish people. This was **an old and widespread form of prejudice** with a long history in Europe, some of which appears earlier in this course: the massacres during the Black Death (7.4), the Venetian ghetto of 1516 and the expulsions of the Reformation era (8.4).

The Nazis did not invent antisemitism. What was new was the **combination of that inherited prejudice with a modern bureaucratic state**, industrial technology, and an explicit programme of extermination.

## The stages of persecution

The process escalated over more than a decade:

1. **Legal exclusion** — laws stripping Jews of citizenship, employment, and rights
2. **Violence** — notably **Kristallnacht**, coordinated violence by Nazis against Jews throughout Germany and Austria
3. **Ghettos, deportation, and isolation**
4. **Internment** — imprisoning people — and **confiscation** of property
5. **The Final Solution** — systematic murder

## The camps

The Nazis operated **five killing centres** — **Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau** — described as **extermination camps** or **death camps**, which murdered Jews using **poison gas**. Other major camps included **Dachau**.

## Who participated

The Holocaust required the involvement of many organisations, not only a small ideological core:

- The **Nazi Party**
- The **SA** (stormtroopers)
- The **SS** (Schutzstaffel, Protection Squadron)
- The **German military**
- The **national railway** — which transported victims
- The **healthcare system** — which administered the earlier programme of murdering disabled people

That list is the most important fact for understanding how it happened. Genocide on this scale required the ordinary institutions of a modern state — timetables, records, budgets — to function normally in the service of it.

## Resistance

Resistance existed despite overwhelming odds, including the **Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (1943)** and, within Germany, the **White Rose** movement.

## Liberation and reckoning

The camps were **liberated by Soviet and Western Allied forces**, and what they found shocked the world.

**War crimes trials** followed: the **Nuremberg Trials (1945–46)** and the **Tokyo Trials** for Japanese crimes. These **set a precedent for international law and for the concept of crimes against humanity** — establishing that following orders is not a defence, and that individuals can be held accountable under international law for acts their own state authorised.

The **creation of Israel in 1948** was influenced in part by sympathy generated by the Holocaust, alongside the longer history of Zionism (1.5).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The Holocaust** | The systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, between 1933 and 1945 |
| **The Shoah** | The Hebrew term for the Holocaust, meaning catastrophe |
| **Antisemitism** | Prejudice against or hatred of Jewish people — an old and widespread form of prejudice with a long history in Europe |
| **Kristallnacht** | Coordinated violence by Nazis against Jews throughout Germany and Austria |
| **Internment** | Imprisoning people |
| **The Final Solution** | Systematic murder — the last stage of the escalating persecution |
| **Extermination camps (death camps)** | The five killing centres — Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau — which murdered Jews using poison gas |
| **SA** | The stormtroopers |
| **SS** | The Schutzstaffel, or Protection Squadron |
| **War crimes trials** | The Nuremberg Trials (1945–46) and the Tokyo Trials for Japanese crimes, which set a precedent for international law and for the concept of crimes against humanity — establishing that following orders is not a defence, and that individuals can be held accountable under international law for acts their own state authorised |

# 4.1 The Cold War Begins

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## An alliance of necessity, 1941–1945

Relations between the United States and the USSR had **always been strained**: the US stood for **capitalism and democracy**, the USSR for **communism and a command economy**. The relationship was further strained by Stalin's decision to sign the **Nazi-Soviet Pact**.

When Germany invaded the USSR, the United States had an opportunity to **use that betrayal to gain an ally** against the Nazis. It sent an aide to assess the Soviet military situation, and **Lend-Lease** provided significant military supplies and other assistance. Stalin left the Axis orbit and joined the Allies.

The alliance was always **against** something rather than **for** anything shared, which is why it did not survive the common enemy.

## The wartime conferences

Victory over the Nazis **did not fix the relationship**:

- The **US** was concerned about the spread of Soviet communism and Stalin's totalitarian rule
- The **USSR** was frustrated by America's hesitance to treat it as part of the international community, and by its slowness in opening a second front

The Allies held two conferences — **Yalta (February 1945)** and **Potsdam (July 1945)** — to decide the fate of Europe, and Germany in particular.

### Points of agreement

1. Germany would be **demilitarised and disarmed**
2. **Denazification**
3. Germans deemed **war criminals** would be arrested and tried
4. Germany would be divided into **four zones of occupation** (US, USSR, Britain, France), with **Berlin** likewise divided into four
5. Countries freed from Nazi control could hold **free, democratic elections**

### Points of disagreement

1. **The boundaries** of the four occupation zones
2. **Reparations.** The USSR wanted a very large sum; the US and Britain believed this **would repeat the mistake of Versailles**, where massive reparations had destabilised Germany and helped cause the next war (1.1)
3. **Poland.** **Harry S. Truman**, the new US president, was frustrated that Stalin began **arresting non-communist Polish leaders** after agreeing to a coalition government

**Potsdam (July 1945)** brought **Truman, Stalin, and Churchill (then Attlee)** together to discuss the post-war order.

## Broken promises, 1945–1947

At Yalta Stalin had promised **free elections and coalition governments**. Between **1945 and 1947 he broke these promises**: communist parties, often backed by Soviet troops, seized control of Eastern European countries including **Poland, Romania, and Hungary**.

The US read this as **expansionist and authoritarian**, feared the ideological spread of communism, and grew increasingly distrustful — the immediate origin of the Cold War.

**The Cold War** is a state of political and military tension after the Second World War between the Western powers and the Eastern bloc, conducted without direct war between the principals. **Proxy wars** — wars between other nations supported by the two sides — were its characteristic form. The **USSR influenced Eastern Europe** while the **USA influenced Western Europe**.

*A counterpoint worth registering:* while the ideological opposition was real, the **power vacuum after 1945** and genuine **security concerns** on both sides also played a large role. The USSR had been invaded through Eastern Europe twice in thirty years, and wanted a buffer.

## Truman Doctrine and containment

In **1947 President Truman** declared a new foreign policy — the **Truman Doctrine**: the United States would **provide political, military, and economic assistance to all nations threatened by communist forces**.

**Before** the doctrine, the US stayed out of regional conflicts that did not directly involve it. **After** it, the US would actively resist communist expansion anywhere. Truman sent military and economic aid to **Greece and Turkey**.

The doctrine was motivated by **containment** — limiting communism to the areas already under Soviet control, rather than attempting to roll it back or ignoring it.

## The Marshall Plan (1947)

A policy of **strengthening democratic governments by providing food and economic assistance** to war-ravaged Europe, motivated by the belief that **countries recovering from the war were vulnerable to communism**.

The USSR saw it as an attempt to **buy the support of smaller countries**. It was offered participation, refused, and **blocked its satellite states** — including East Germany and Poland — from benefiting.

The Marshall Plan is the economic arm of containment, and the more effective one: prosperity in Western Europe did more to prevent communist electoral success there than any military measure.

## NATO and the Warsaw Pact

**NATO (1949).** The United States, Canada, and ten other countries formed the **North Atlantic Treaty Organization**, whose members agreed to **protect one another if any were attacked**.

**The Warsaw Pact (1955).** The USSR responded by creating its own alliance, comprising the USSR and **seven satellite states** in Eastern Europe. A **satellite state** is formally independent but under heavy political, economic, and military control by another country.

The two were not symmetrical: **NATO functioned as an alliance**, while the USSR **used the Warsaw Pact to control its satellite states** — as Hungary discovered in 1956.

## The early Cold War, 1948–1961

### The Berlin Blockade (1948–49)

Berlin lay **inside Soviet-controlled eastern Germany**, but the US and its allies controlled the western portions of the city — an anomaly that raised the question of whether those portions would be absorbed into East Germany.

On **24 June 1948** Soviet forces **blockaded rail, road, and water access** to the Allied sectors, attempting to force the Allies out. The **US and UK responded by airlifting food and fuel** into the city.

The Soviets lifted the land blockade on **12 May 1949**. **Berlin remained divided for the rest of the Cold War.**

The airlift is the model Cold War confrontation: an enormous, sustained, and expensive operation designed specifically to **avoid firing a shot** while refusing to concede.

### The Hungarian Revolution (1956)

A spontaneous nationwide revolt against Hungary's communist government and against Soviet domination. It began as a **student demonstration**; a student delegation entering the radio building to broadcast their demands was detained, and demonstrators outside demanded their release. News spread quickly, and disorder and violence erupted throughout the capital.

Thousands organised into **militias**, battling the **State Security Police (ÁVH)** and Soviet troops. Pro-Soviet communists and ÁVH members were often executed or imprisoned as former prisoners were released and armed.

A new government formed, declared its intention to **withdraw from the Warsaw Pact**, and pledged **free elections**. After first announcing a willingness to negotiate a Soviet withdrawal, the USSR **changed its mind and crushed the revolution**, following it with **mass executions and imprisonment**.

Hungary demonstrated the limits of Western support: containment meant preventing communism from spreading, not liberating countries already inside the Soviet sphere.

### The Berlin Wall

The Wall was a long separation barrier between **West Berlin and East Germany**, built during the post-war division.

Its cause was **defection**. East Germans crossed into West Berlin daily, including skilled workers and professionals — a **brain drain** representing a serious economic loss, and driven by both political and economic motives.

Its effect was symbolic as well as physical: the Wall **symbolised communist repression in the West**, and the **shooting of defectors damaged East Germany's image** severely. A state that must wall its citizens in makes an argument against itself that no propaganda can answer.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lend-Lease** | The programme that provided the USSR with significant military supplies and other assistance |
| **Yalta (February 1945)** | The conference held to decide the fate of Europe, and Germany in particular, at which Stalin promised free elections and coalition governments |
| **Potsdam (July 1945)** | The conference bringing Truman, Stalin, and Churchill (then Attlee) together to discuss the post-war order |
| **The Cold War** | A state of political and military tension after the Second World War between the Western powers and the Eastern bloc, conducted without direct war between the principals |
| **Proxy wars** | Wars between other nations supported by the two sides — the characteristic form of the Cold War |
| **Truman Doctrine** | Truman's 1947 foreign policy: the United States would provide political, military, and economic assistance to all nations threatened by communist forces |
| **Containment** | Limiting communism to the areas already under Soviet control, rather than attempting to roll it back or ignoring it |
| **The Marshall Plan (1947)** | A policy of strengthening democratic governments by providing food and economic assistance to war-ravaged Europe, motivated by the belief that countries recovering from the war were vulnerable to communism |
| **NATO (1949)** | The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, formed by the United States, Canada, and ten other countries, whose members agreed to protect one another if any were attacked |
| **The Warsaw Pact (1955)** | The alliance the USSR created in response to NATO, comprising the USSR and seven satellite states in Eastern Europe, and used to control them |
| **Satellite state** | A state formally independent but under heavy political, economic, and military control by another country |
| **The Berlin Blockade (1948–49)** | The Soviet blockade of rail, road, and water access to the Allied sectors of Berlin from 24 June 1948, attempting to force the Allies out; the US and UK responded by airlifting food and fuel into the city, and the land blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949 |
| **The Hungarian Revolution (1956)** | A spontaneous nationwide revolt against Hungary's communist government and against Soviet domination, crushed by the USSR and followed by mass executions and imprisonment |
| **State Security Police (ÁVH)** | The Hungarian security police, battled by the militias of the 1956 revolution alongside Soviet troops |
| **The Berlin Wall** | A long separation barrier between West Berlin and East Germany, built during the post-war division |
| **Brain drain** | The daily loss of East Germans — including skilled workers and professionals — into West Berlin, a serious economic loss driven by both political and economic motives |

# 5.1 The Vietnam War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The Vietnam War is the clearest test case of **containment** (4.1), and the place where it failed.

## Origins

Vietnam had been a **French colony** before Japanese occupation during the Second World War. Afterwards it was **returned to French control**, but many Vietnamese wanted independence.

By **1950** the French were fighting the **Viet Minh**, an organisation dedicated to removing foreign imperialist powers from Vietnam. The **USA began to bankroll the French war effort**, worried about the spread of communism in Southeast Asia under the **Truman Doctrine**.

Note the tension in the American position from the outset: the US was funding a **European colonial power** against an **independence movement**, in the name of anti-communism.

**In 1954 the French were defeated at Dien Bien Phu.** The defeat was formalised in the **Geneva Agreement**, which **temporarily divided Vietnam** into a northern zone governed by the Viet Minh and a southern zone. This marked the **end of French control** and the beginning of a major dilemma for American leaders.

The North Vietnamese government, led by **Ho Chi Minh**, declared a socialist state in **1954**. An **election was scheduled for 1956** to decide whether the country would reunify.

Ho Chi Minh's government attempted to remain neutral and socialist but ended up **allying with communist China** — which the US took as proof that North Vietnam was communist.

## Domino theory and escalation

America operated a policy of **containment** and feared that if Vietnam fell to communism, other countries in Southeast Asia would follow — the **domino theory**.

The US therefore supported the anti-communist South Vietnamese dictator **Ngo Dinh Diem**, who **refused to hold the 1956 elections** that might have unified the country under Ho Chi Minh. Many South Vietnamese who supported reunification joined an armed uprising against Diem.

**The Vietcong** were supported and supplied by North Vietnam. Their message of **independence from foreign control and land reform** appealed to peasant farmers — an appeal the US never matched.

**In 1962 Diem introduced the Strategic Hamlets policy**, isolating villagers from Vietcong influence by **destroying villages near Vietcong areas and forcibly relocating the population**. It **backfired**, making Diem deeply unpopular and **increasing support for the Vietcong**. This is the war's recurring pattern: measures intended to separate the population from the insurgency drove them toward it.

**In 1959 Ho Chi Minh declared war** to overthrow South Vietnam's government and unite the country under communism, and the Vietcong launched a **guerrilla war**.

Under **Eisenhower and Kennedy** the USA spent millions supporting the effort. These attempts failed, and **direct military force** came to be seen as necessary.

**Diem was assassinated in November 1963** after a military coup, which gave the USA an excuse to intervene more directly under the banner of restoring stability.

**In August 1964** the **USS Maddox** was attacked by North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the **Gulf of Tonkin**, provoking **President Johnson** into military retaliation and beginning direct US involvement.

## Why the Vietcong succeeded

**Guerrilla warfare.** They used **jungle cover and local knowledge to strike and vanish**, fighting **hit-and-run** actions against often young, inexperienced US conscripts. **Booby traps**, including punji sticks, caused physical and **psychological** damage.

**The Ho Chi Minh Trail** was the vital supply route from North Vietnam, running through **Laos and Cambodia** — outside South Vietnam, and therefore politically difficult to attack.

**The Tet Offensive (1968).** A surprise attack during the **Tet** (New Year) holiday on US-held positions. Though the attack was eventually **pushed back militarily**, it **shattered American confidence** and proved that the US was **not winning** despite an enormous investment of troops, bombs, and money.

Tet is the crucial episode because it separates **military outcome** from **political outcome**. The US won the battle and lost the war's public support in the same month.

## Why US strategy failed

**Military technology and chemical warfare.** The US used **high-altitude bombers, jets, napalm** (which burned skin to bone), and **Agent Orange** (a jungle defoliant).

**Failure of Operation Rolling Thunder.** Bombs often **missed their targets**, falling into empty jungle.

**Failure of Search and Destroy.** Missions relied on **poor military intelligence**, and produced atrocities including the **My Lai Massacre**.

**The role of the media.** Graphic coverage — burning homes, napalm victims — **shocked Americans** and turned opinion against the war. Vietnam was the first war reported nightly on television.

**Lack of support at home.** Anti-war sentiment grew as the war dragged on. In **1970 the National Guard killed four students at Kent State University**, increasing public anger further.

## Ending the war

**Johnson stepped down.** By 1968 criticism of the war had increased in the USA and internationally.

**Vietnamisation (the Nixon Doctrine, 1969).** Though anti-communist, **Nixon feared the risk of nuclear war** and aimed to ease Cold War tensions. Under the Nixon Doctrine, **US troops would only be used if the country was directly threatened**, with the fighting handed back to South Vietnamese forces.

Nixon also **bombed Vietcong bases in Laos and Cambodia**, aiming to pressure North Vietnam into serious negotiations. **Bombing continued even while peace talks were ongoing or had broken down.**

**The Paris Peace Accords (1973).** Pressure for peace came from **growing public opposition**, from the **Nixon Doctrine**, and from **Nixon's desire to improve relations with China and the USSR**, which reduced his interest in anti-communist military action.

In **October 1972 Henry Kissinger** reached a draft deal with North Vietnam. **Nguyen Van Thieu**, South Vietnam's president, **refused to sign**, fearing American abandonment. Nixon played "bad cop", threatening him and launching massive bombing campaigns on North Vietnam.

A **ceasefire** was agreed. The **final US evacuation was chaotic** — helicopters lifting personnel and civilians from rooftops to navy ships.

## Consequences

**Military failure of containment.** Despite overwhelming military strength, the US failed to stop communism in Vietnam.

**Political failure of containment.** Vietnam fell to communism, and **US bombing in Laos and Cambodia helped communist regimes rise there too** — the domino theory partly vindicated, by American action.

**Moral cost.** The war was presented as a moral fight against communism, but **atrocities** — civilian killings, chemical warfare — severely damaged America's global image.

**Human and financial cost.** **58,000 American deaths** and **1–4 million Vietnamese deaths**.

**New foreign policy direction.** **Containment was abandoned**, and the USA entered a period of **détente** — a thaw in Cold War tensions with the USSR and China.

| **Geneva Agreement** | The agreement formalising the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, which temporarily divided Vietnam into a northern zone governed by the Viet Minh and a southern zone, marking the end of French control |
| **Domino theory** | The fear that if Vietnam fell to communism, other countries in Southeast Asia would follow |
| **The Vietcong** | The armed uprising against Diem, supported and supplied by North Vietnam, whose message of independence from foreign control and land reform appealed to peasant farmers |
| **Strategic Hamlets policy (1962)** | Diem's policy of isolating villagers from Vietcong influence by destroying villages near Vietcong areas and forcibly relocating the population |
| **Gulf of Tonkin (August 1964)** | The attack on the USS Maddox by North Vietnamese torpedo boats, which provoked President Johnson into military retaliation and began direct US involvement |
| **Guerrilla warfare** | Using jungle cover and local knowledge to strike and vanish, fighting hit-and-run actions |

# 1 Causes of the Second World War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide gives six causes. The first five run in sequence — each one makes the
next more likely — and the sixth is a set of longer-term conditions carried over
from the First World War.

## 1. Unresolved problems from the Treaty of Versailles

Germany and its allies were held **responsible for all destruction and costs**
of the First World War. Under the Treaty they **lost territory**, were forced to
pay **huge reparations**, had to accept responsibility through the **war guilt
clause**, and were forced to **demilitarise**.

The consequences followed directly from the reparations: Germany could not pay
them, and so suffered **inflation and unemployment**. Germany felt **bitter and
desperate**, wanting its freedom and territory back — which became a strong
ambition to make a comeback.

## 2. The Great Depression and the rise of dictatorships

The American **Wall Street Crash of October 1929** set off a chain reaction.
Because America needed to service its own debts, Germany could no longer seek
financial support to pay reparations, and France and Britain in turn stopped
making their loan payments to Germany.

While sitting governments proved unable to revive their countries,
**totalitarian leaders** rose instead. **Totalitarianism** is a system of
government in which one party tries to rule with complete control over every
aspect of its citizens' lives.

| Leader | Country | System |
|---|---|---|
| **Joseph Stalin** | USSR | Communist |
| **Adolf Hitler** | Germany | Fascism |
| **Benito Mussolini** | Italy | Fascism |
| **Emperor Hirohito** | Japan | Constitutional monarch |

Their ideologies differed, but all four drove towards **militarism and
nationalism** — and those are the factors that led them to demand control over
other nations aggressively.

## 3. Failure of the League of Nations

The **League of Nations** was an international forum and a collective security
arrangement: member nations agreed to **settle disputes rather than go to war**.

It is judged a failure on four counts:

- The **United States, a major power, refused to join**, and other countries
  grew suspicious as a result
- In **1931 Japan invaded Manchuria** (north-eastern China) and the League did
  not stop it
- In **1935 Italy invaded Abyssinia** (present-day Ethiopia) and, rather than
  helping, **Britain and France signed a secret pact** handing Abyssinia to Italy
- **Germany left the League and rearmed**; the League called a disarmament
  conference and Germany ignored it, moving instead to regain territories such
  as the **Rhineland**

The outcome was severe **distrust between nations**: small nations were
neglected and many countries simply disobeyed the League's rules.

## 4. Appeasement (1935–1939)

Britain and France judged that conflict with Germany would produce a
devastating war like the First World War. The policy was carried out mainly by
British Prime Minister **Neville Chamberlain**.

Two reasons are given: **Britain was not prepared for war**, and some felt
**sympathetic towards Hitler and his complaints**. Appeasement meant granting
Hitler land, control over nations, and the freedom to remilitarise.

The **Munich Agreement** is the clearest example. Britain and France willingly
gave Germany the **Sudetenland** — western Czechoslovakia, which had a
German-speaking population — on the condition that Hitler promised to go no
further. German citizens found this reasonable because Hitler claimed he wanted
to **unite all German-speaking people into the Third Reich**.

**Anschluss** was also created: a union between **Austria and Germany in 1938**,
dedicated to Germany's future expansion, because Austria supplied strategic
land, resources and soldiers adequate for German exploitation.

Chamberlain was confident Britain would now be at peace. **Winston Churchill**
strongly opposed appeasement, knowing Hitler would not stop after annexing the
Sudetenland. Appeasement therefore caused the war: Hitler **developed
unstoppable hubris** and became more demanding still.

## 5. The invasion of Poland

This is the **official and direct cause** of the war.

Britain, France and Russia had previously formed an alliance, the Allied
powers. In **August 1939 Russia left it and joined Hitler**, signing the
**Nazi–Soviet Pact** — a non-aggression pact publicly stating that the rival
nations would maintain peaceful relations. They agreed to divide Poland into
**spheres of influence**: Germany taking western Poland, the USSR the east.

On **1 September 1939** Germany invaded Poland using **blitzkrieg** — lightning
war, defeating opponents through a series of short military campaigns — which
caused immediate harm to Poland and is how Germany won. Germany's **Luftwaffe**
was a critical part of blitzkrieg. On **17 September 1939** the USSR occupied
eastern Poland.

Poland's position was **geographically vulnerable**, lying directly between the
USSR and Germany.

Hitler claimed that ethnic Germans living in Poland needed protection, which
served as his excuse to invade. Britain and France declared war, having
recognised that appeasement had failed. Hitler had **panzers** (tanks) and a
well-trained army, built secretly over the preceding years in violation of the
Treaty of Versailles.

## 6. Other causes, shared with the First World War

**M.A.I.N.** — **M**ilitarism, **A**lliances, **I**mperialism, **N**ationalism.

The alliances were:

| Bloc | Members |
|---|---|
| **Axis powers** | Germany, Italy, Japan |
| **Allied powers** | United States, Britain, France |

The **USSR** was originally allied with the Axis powers, until Germany invaded
it in **1941**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **War guilt clause** | The Treaty of Versailles term making Germany accept responsibility for the First World War |
| **Totalitarianism** | A system in which one party rules with complete control over every aspect of citizens' lives |
| **League of Nations** | An international forum and collective security arrangement whose members agreed to settle disputes rather than go to war |
| **Appeasement** | Granting Hitler land, control over nations and freedom to remilitarise in order to avoid war |
| **Munich Agreement** | The agreement giving Germany the Sudetenland on Hitler's promise to go no further |
| **Sudetenland** | Western Czechoslovakia, which had a German-speaking population |
| **Anschluss** | The 1938 union between Austria and Germany, dedicated to Germany's future expansion |
| **Nazi–Soviet Pact** | The August 1939 non-aggression pact dividing Poland into German and Soviet spheres of influence |
| **Blitzkrieg** | Lightning war: defeating opponents through a series of short military campaigns |
| **Luftwaffe** | The German air force, a critical part of blitzkrieg |
| **Panzers** | German tanks |
| **M.A.I.N.** | Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism |

# 2 The Two Theatres of the War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The war was fought in two theatres, the **Pacific** and the **European**. The
guide gives an estimated **65 million total deaths worldwide**, of which
**40 million were civilians**.

## European theatre: significant statistics

- **150 trillion** ways for the German **Enigma** machine to encode a single letter
- **400,000 tons** of supplies delivered to the Allied front in France
- **9.5 million** estimated peak strength of the German armed forces
- **7,600** Women's Army Corps members serving in the European theatre by 1945,
  which the guide reads as portraying women's increasing authority

## Pacific theatre: significant statistics

- **3 atomic bombs** detonated by the United States during the war
- **115,000 square miles** of ocean covered in battles
- **20 million** estimated deaths in China as a result of the war — China
  contributed by resisting Japanese aggression, on the Allied side

## Comparing the two

The three comparisons are not independent: the geography determines which
technology is useful, and the technology in turn shapes the casualty figures.

| | European theatre | Pacific theatre |
|---|---|---|
| **Geography** | Dense continent, land-based | Vast oceans and island chains; naval and marine-based, US-led |
| **Military technology** | Tanks, artillery, machine guns, code breaking (German Enigma), V2 rockets | Aircraft carriers, nuclear bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, submarines, planes |
| **Military deaths** | 15–20 million | 4 million |
| **Civilian deaths** | 30–35 million | 10–12 million |

The European theatre was **more deadly** on both counts.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Enigma** | The German encoding machine, with 150 trillion ways to encode a single letter |
| **Women's Army Corps** | The women's branch serving in the European theatre, 7,600 strong by 1945 |

# 3 The United States Enters the War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why the United States stayed out

Two conditions produced a **mood of isolationism** in which the country did not
want to intervene in any more bloody conflicts: the **Great Depression**, which
brought severe economic damage and political instability, and the **trauma of
the First World War**.

**Woodrow Wilson**, the previous president, had wanted to join the League of
Nations but was blocked by Congress. He was replaced by **Warren G. Harding**,
who refused to join any war — aligning with what citizens wanted — claiming the
country needed to **return to normalcy**.

The **Neutrality Acts**, passed by Congress after the failure of the League of
Nations, **banned American citizens from trading with nations at war, loaning
them money, or travelling on their ships**. The United States believed no nation
posed a direct threat.

## Getting indirectly involved

President **Franklin Delano Roosevelt**, in office from **1933**, pressed for
participation, but the Neutrality Acts limited him, so he moved to involve the
country indirectly first. Three steps followed:

The guide dates his push to 1932; that is an error — Roosevelt was not yet
president in 1932, and the war he wanted to join did not begin until 1939.

- **November 1939** — American manufacturers were allowed to sell arms and
  supplies to nations at war. The British could buy American goods provided they
  **paid up front and carried them in their own ships**
- **March 1941** — after Hitler had conquered France and Britain was the *one man
  standing*, Congress passed the **Lend-Lease Act**, authorising the United
  States to lend war supplies to any nation whose defence Roosevelt deemed
  **vital to the defence of the United States**. He argued the best policy for
  keeping the country out of war was to become the **Arsenal of Democracy**
- **August 1941** — Roosevelt and Churchill met on the **Atlantic Charter**,
  which set out their desire to preserve peace and their commitment to working
  together in the war

Each step moves further from neutrality while stopping short of fighting: sale
for cash, then lending, then a joint statement of war aims.

## Getting directly involved

On **7 December 1941** Japanese carrier planes attacked the American fleet at
**Pearl Harbor**, Hawaii, knocking out the pride of the US Pacific fleet. One
day later Congress declared war on Japan, and Italy and Germany declared war on
the United States.

The Allied response was the **Germany first strategy**, agreed by Churchill and
Roosevelt: although Japan had made the attack, **Germany was the more
threatening enemy**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Isolationism** | The mood in which the United States did not want to intervene in further conflicts |
| **Return to normalcy** | Harding's claim in refusing to join the war |
| **Neutrality Acts** | Acts banning Americans from trading with, lending to, or travelling on the ships of nations at war |
| **Lend-Lease Act** | The March 1941 act authorising the US to lend war supplies to nations vital to its own defence |
| **Arsenal of Democracy** | Roosevelt's phrase for supplying the Allies as the best way to stay out of the war |
| **Atlantic Charter** | The August 1941 Roosevelt–Churchill statement of peace aims and wartime cooperation |
| **Germany first strategy** | The Allied decision to treat Germany as the greater threat despite Japan's attack |

# 4 The Eastern Front: Operation Barbarossa and Stalingrad

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**More combatants were killed on the Eastern Front than in all other theatres of
the war combined.**

## The ideological groundwork

Hitler wrote ***Mein Kampf*** — *My Struggle* — in **1924–25**, publishing the
first volume in **1925**. It set out
**territorial expansion, a racially pure state, and the destruction of Jews**,
laying the ideological groundwork for the Holocaust.

The guide dates the book to 1923; that is an error — 1923 is the year of the
Beer Hall Putsch, after which Hitler wrote it in prison.

He believed Germany was destined to defeat its historic enemy, **France**, and
then push eastward into the **USSR** to exterminate communists and Slavs. He also
knew that **fighting both at once was not feasible** — and that constraint is
what produced the pact that follows.

In **August 1939** Hitler therefore signed the **Nazi–Soviet Pact**, dividing
Poland, the Baltic States (Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia), Romania and Finland into
German and Soviet spheres of influence, Germany taking western Poland and the
USSR the east. Strategically he was befriending the USSR in order to **avoid
conflict with it while seizing Poland and France**, saying *the sooner Russia is
smashed the better*. What he wanted from the eventual attack was to
**exterminate Slavs, exterminate communism, and gain access to valuable
resources**. In **September 1939** Germany and the USSR both invaded Poland.

## Operation Barbarossa

On **22 June 1941** Hitler launched **Operation Barbarossa**, a **three million
man invasion** of the USSR. He was hubristic, believing the USSR would be easy to
defeat because its generals were inept and there was political instability, some
opposing Stalin's regime.

It succeeded in the early stages, but the **Red Army** — led by the
Bolsheviks — made a major comeback, being the largest army in the world with
vast natural resources, and won. The United States and the United Kingdom then
united with the USSR, since they shared a common enemy in Nazi Germany, and
together fought at **Stalingrad**.

## Conditions

Atrocities including beheadings and mass rapes occurred daily, and millions of
captured soldiers died of exposure and maltreatment in inhumane conditions.

Hitler's defeat came largely from **overwhelming determination — a refusal to
retreat despite substantial casualties**. In late 1942 General **Blumentritt**,
after visiting the Eastern Front, reported that *there was little timber
available for constructing defenses, there were no proper trenches or fixed
positions*, and suggested a step back; Hitler ignored him. Soldiers in 1942–1943
said *I would eat a cat* and *this isn't hell, this is ten times worse than
hell*. An arctic winter stopped the German advance **before Moscow**.

Both sides showed strong nationalism and dedication. On **28 July 1942** Hitler
wanted to wipe out the males and deport the females, while the Russian General
**Chuikov** said *we will defend the city or die*.

| Side | Deaths |
|---|---|
| **Axis powers** | 850,000 |
| **Soviets** | 750,000 |

**Significance:** Stalingrad marked **Hitler's first major defeat** and a shift
in alliance, with the **USSR joining the Allied powers**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| ***Mein Kampf*** | Hitler's book setting out territorial expansion, a racially pure state and the destruction of Jews |
| **Operation Barbarossa** | The 22 June 1941 three-million-man German invasion of the USSR |
| **Red Army** | The Soviet army, led by the Bolsheviks and the largest in the world |
| **Battle of Stalingrad** | Hitler's first major defeat, after which the USSR joined the Allies |

# 5 The War in the European Theatre, 1941–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The campaigns run in sequence, each one opening the way to the next: North
Africa clears the Mediterranean, Sicily opens Italy, Italy draws German troops
south, and Normandy opens the second front.

## Mid-1942: the German First strategy

The Allies reached consensus that **Japan was a much smaller threat than
Germany**.

## November 1942: Operation Torch — the invasion of North Africa

The original plan was for Generals **George Marshall** and **Dwight Eisenhower**
to invade German-occupied France directly, distracting German troops from the
USSR by opening a second front. That was **not feasible because the US army had
not mobilised**, so North Africa was attacked instead. It was Eisenhower's
**first combat assignment**.

The Allies landed in **Morocco and Algeria**, then moved east towards **Tunisia**.
They suffered setbacks at the **Kasserine Pass** in February 1943, but within two
months had trapped numerous Axis troops. They won.

## January 1943: the Casablanca Conference

Held in Casablanca, north-west Morocco, near the end of Operation Torch, where
Roosevelt and Churchill met to decide future military plans. The outcomes were
to **pursue the unconditional surrender of the Axis powers**, and to **invade
Sicily first, then mainland Italy**.

## July–September 1943: Sicily (Operation Husky) and Italy

Under Generals **George Patton** and **Montgomery**. **Sicily surrendered
immediately**, but Hitler ordered his forces to **fight to the last man** to hold
Italy.

The Allies then bombed **Berlin** — Nazi production centres — nearly annihilating
the **Luftwaffe**, which was crucial to the success of D-Day, and also bombed
Belgium and northern France. Going into the Berlin raids the Allies knew they
faced **the most powerful air defence system in the world**. **Dogfighting** is
close combat between military aircraft.

## June 1944: the invasion of Italy

**Kesselring** led the German defence, driving the Allied invasion force back
into the sea at **Salerno**, in the south of Italy. His key strategy was the
**Gustav Line**: a defensive entanglement of machine guns, booby traps and mines
stitched into Italy's mountains. On **4 June** the Allies took **Rome**.

## 6 June 1944: D-Day — the invasion of Normandy

**Operation Overlord**, the **largest amphibious** — land and water — **operation
of the war**.

It succeeded because the Allies **invaded by surprise**, landing at **Normandy
instead of Calais**, where the Channel was far narrower and Axis defences
stronger. Under Eisenhower, Allied forces liberated **Paris and northern France
and Belgium**.

**The liberation of Paris:** on **25 August 1944** Germany surrendered Paris to
the Allies. This opened the **western front**, forcing Germany to fight in both
east and west. Allied advances then slowed, because the Allies disagreed among
themselves over strategy — between indirect and direct approaches — which slowed
decision-making and delayed offensives.

### Specifics of the landing

Conditions were harsh: the English Channel had rough seas, unpredictable weather
and formidable beach obstacles. Before the war one participant said *we were
getting ready for one of the biggest adventures of our lives*.

At midnight on 6 June the Allies began by **sabotaging bridges and railway
lines** to prevent an Axis defence, then landed the largest amphibious force,
moving through storm-tossed waters towards the beaches. Americans were packed
into flat-bottomed **Higgins boats**, with vomit filling the bottoms.

| Beaches | Forces |
|---|---|
| **Juno, Gold, Sword** | British and Canadian |
| **Omaha, Utah** | American |

**Omaha** saw the fiercest fighting because of its steep cliffs; the Americans
took it at heavy cost, with a **loss rate above 13%**. An artillery battalion
member said *if you thought about the possibilities of what lay ahead, it was
more than your mind could take*.

**Red Ball Express** was an American truck convoy system operating 24 hours a
day, with **many African American drivers**, supplying fuel, ammunition and other
vital supplies to Allied forces advancing through France and Belgium after
Normandy. It was named for the **red balls** marking its designated routes and
labelling its trucks, so that people could free up the roads for oncoming troops.

**Significance:** had D-Day failed, no further attempt would have been possible
for another year, giving Hitler time to strengthen the **Atlantic Wall** and
harass England with the newly developed **V1 flying bombs and V2 rockets**.

## September 1944: Operation Market Garden — a failure

A flawed plan to capture key bridges in the **Netherlands** and enter Germany
quickly. The Allies attempted to break into the heart of Germany but took losses
for small gains: *the wrong time, the wrong place* — Germany was fully equipped.
Over **250 aircraft** were shot down.

## 16 December 1944: the Battle of the Bulge

The **largest American infantry battle** of the war. Hitler launched panzer units
through the **Ardennes Forest**, pushing the Allies back far enough to create a
**bulge** in their defensive line.

The Allies came back when the skies cleared before Christmas, letting their
strong aircraft pound the invading army — the United States was known for
powerful air forces, having fought Japan in the Pacific. The Allies pushed the
Germans back across the **Rhine**.

This was **a soldier's fight without much direction from leaders**: guts,
self-respect and loyalty to comrades prevailed over ideology. The Allies won, at
a cost of **19,000 American GIs killed** against **100,000 German dead**.

It marked the **official beginning of the fall of the German empire**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Operation Torch** | The November 1942 Allied invasion of North Africa, Eisenhower's first combat assignment |
| **Casablanca Conference** | The January 1943 meeting deciding to pursue unconditional Axis surrender and invade Sicily first |
| **Operation Husky** | The July–September 1943 invasion of Sicily |
| **Dogfighting** | Close combat between military aircraft |
| **Gustav Line** | Kesselring's defensive entanglement of machine guns, booby traps and mines in Italy's mountains |
| **Operation Overlord** | D-Day, the 6 June 1944 invasion of Normandy and largest amphibious operation of the war |
| **Amphibious** | Combining land and water operations |
| **Higgins boats** | The flat-bottomed landing craft carrying American troops to the beaches |
| **Red Ball Express** | The 24-hour American truck convoy system, with many African American drivers, supplying the advance through France and Belgium |
| **Atlantic Wall** | The German coastal defences D-Day's failure would have allowed Hitler to strengthen |
| **Operation Market Garden** | The failed September 1944 plan to capture bridges in the Netherlands and enter Germany |
| **Battle of the Bulge** | The largest American infantry battle, marking the official beginning of the fall of the German empire |

# 6 The War in the Pacific Theatre, 1941–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## 7 December 1941: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor

The attack **severely crippled the US Pacific fleet**. Because the battleship
fleet in Hawaii was crippled, the United States had to rely on **aircraft
carriers and submarines** instead — which is why the carrier battles that follow
were decisive. Japan's aim was to **destroy the US carrier fleet** so that it
could negotiate for peace.

Between the set-piece battles, Allied forces repeatedly bombed and stormed
Japanese-held territory, targeting tiny islands as well as the jungles of New
Guinea and the Philippines, with the goal of **securing airfields and supply
bases that could serve as launching points for future attacks**.

## May 1942: the Battle of the Coral Sea

Both sides suffered enormous losses, but it was a definite win for the United
States and marked **the first defeat for Japan**. The guide describes it as
ending the peak of Japan.

## June 1942: the Battle of Midway

The **turning point**. The United States prevailed and took the offensive for the
first time, in its **first major victory against Japan**, destroying **four
Japanese aircraft carriers**.

## August 1942: Guadalcanal and the Solomon Islands

The Allies took the **first vital step in driving the Japanese back** in the
Pacific. Its significance is that the United States **prevented Japanese efforts
to disrupt US supply routes to Australia and New Zealand**. **William Douglas
Lansford** took part in this combat.

## March 1943: the island-hopping strategy

**Island hopping** is the practice of **skipping over heavily fortified islands
in order to seize lightly defended locations that could support the next
advance**. It turned the vastness of the Pacific into an American ally, letting
the United States leapfrog across it.

In practice, General **Douglas MacArthur**'s troops first captured **New Guinea**,
but found the heavily defended island of **Rabaul** formidable, so the fleets
pushed westwards to invade less-defended islands first — and eventually captured
Rabaul successfully. It worked because, while MacArthur was island hopping in the
south-west Pacific, there were simultaneous central Pacific campaigns invading
the **Gilbert Islands** in November 1943; with two assaults to face, Japan
crashed out.

## January–February 1944: the Mariana Islands

**Key for the invasion of mainland Japan.** The Marianas were a particularly
valuable asset because they were **close enough to Japan for the new US B-29
bombers to reach the mainland**.

## February–April 1945: Iwo Jima and Okinawa

### Iwo Jima

It was attacked because it was a **strategic air base located between the Mariana
Islands and Japan**.

The Japanese had **carved out underground fortifications**, turning the volcanic
island into a death trap for invading US marines. US planners expected only brief
campaigns; it lasted **over five weeks**. The Japanese commander General
**Kuribayashi** concentrated his forces in northern Iwo Jima, which made the
battle very bloody. Two names capture its brutality: **the meat grinder**, where
850 US marines died, and **bloody gorge**, where the Japanese defenders made their
final stand. The United States eventually took the island.

As a **symbol of nationalism**, on **23 February 1945** US troops reaching **Mount
Suribachi** raised a small American flag, then returned to replace it with a
larger one — producing one of the most notable photographs of the war.

**William Douglas Lansford** also fought here, in the field-intelligence unit;
afterwards he worked as a Hollywood screenwriter and published books on the war
and his experiences. **Howard N. McLaughlin** fought here in the repair section
for heavy equipment, and later joined the front line because of a shortage of
soldiers. In his memoir he wrote of the marines' feelings towards the Japanese:
*they neither liked or hated the Japs. They killed them without anger or mercy.
To them they were part of the forces of evil that had to be destroyed*.

### Okinawa

On **1 April 1945** the US Tenth Army arrived at Okinawa, the **last invasion
before mainland Japan**. Conditions were harsh, with heavy rains and rugged
terrain.

The United States overcame **northern Okinawa easily by 18 April**, but the south
was **difficult** because the Japanese had anchored their defences at **Shuri
Castle** behind a series of well-defended high ridges. On **29 May** the United
States finally smashed down Shuri Castle.

From **26 March**, **kamikaze** pilots deliberately crashed their planes into US
aircraft carriers and other battleships.

| Side | Deaths |
|---|---|
| **American** | 1,200, including the Tenth Army's commander Lieutenant General Simon Buckner |
| **Japanese** | About 90,000 combatants and 150,000 civilians |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battle of Midway** | The June 1942 turning point and first major US victory, destroying four Japanese carriers |
| **Island hopping** | Skipping heavily fortified islands to seize lightly defended ones that could support the next advance |
| **Mariana Islands** | Islands close enough to Japan for the new B-29 bombers to reach the mainland |
| **The meat grinder** | The name given to the Iwo Jima fighting in which 850 US marines died |
| **Bloody gorge** | Where the Japanese defenders of Iwo Jima made their final stand |
| **Shuri Castle** | The anchor of the Japanese defence in southern Okinawa |
| **Kamikaze** | Japanese pilots who deliberately crashed their planes into US ships |

# 7 The End of the War, 1944–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The Allied position throughout was that *the only solution to this war is
Germany's unconditional surrender*.

## The European theatre

Three developments brought the war in Europe to an end.

**1. Operation Overlord (June 1944) and the Battle of the Bulge (December
1944).** D-Day marked the beginning of the Allied effort to liberate western
Europe from Hitler; after pushing eastward the Allies fought the Battle of the
Bulge.

**2. Soviet advance from the east.** After winning at **Stalingrad and Kursk** in
south-west Russia in 1943, the USSR reached Poland by 1945 and **conquered
Berlin**. On the way it **liberated concentration camps such as Auschwitz**, which
Allied soldiers found spine-chilling.

**3. The link-up on the Elbe.** On **25 April 1945** American and Soviet troops
converged on the **Elbe River near Torgau**, and both sides knew the end of the war
was days away.

> The guide dates this meeting to April 1944. Its own sequence places it after
> the December 1944 Bulge and the 1945 fall of Berlin, so 1945 is the year the
> guide's own account requires.

### Why Hitler lost so badly

Rather than surrendering when there was clearly no turning back, he **pulled
grandfathers and children into the war** under the order to *fight to the last
man*. German soldiers, however, surrendered. When he finally recognised his
failure he **took his own life**, after which a German general signed the
**unconditional surrender** with the Allies.

**8 May 1945** was **V-E Day** — Victory in Europe Day — when the Allies
celebrated, and it is the date the war in Europe formally ended.

The guide heads this section "officially ended on May 2nd 1945" and then gives 8
May as V-E Day; the two do not agree. **2 May** is the day the Berlin garrison
surrendered, not the end of the war in Europe — take 8 May as the end date.

## The Pacific theatre

In May 1945 the Allies remained sceptical, because **Japan had never declared
surrender** and might attack again. Five events followed in quick succession:

- **6 August** — the United States dropped an atomic bomb on **Hiroshima**,
  killing **140,000 people**
- The **USSR declared war on Japan** and the Red Army took **Manchuria**. Japan
  now faced more enemies, which contributed to its surrender
- **9 August** — the United States dropped an atomic bomb on **Nagasaki**, killing
  **70,000 people**
- **14 August** — Japan surrendered at the **Potsdam Conference**. This was
  **V-J Day for Americans**, and celebration erupted across the United States
- **2 September** — the official time for celebration, late because this was the
  day the formal surrender documents were signed aboard the **USS Missouri** in
  Tokyo Bay: fireworks, confetti, parades, and American flags hung up in New York's
  Times Square

In **Honolulu**, veterans and their girlfriends crowded onto trucks and drove
around. **15 August** was **Britain's V-J Day**, later than the American one
because the Americans wanted to join it.

## The brutality of the war

*It was too much death to contemplate, too much savagery and suffering.* The
total was **65 million deaths worldwide**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unconditional surrender** | The Allied condition for ending the war, requiring no negotiated terms |
| **V-E Day** | Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945 |
| **V-J Day** | Victory over Japan Day: 14 August for Americans, 15 August for Britain |
| **Potsdam Conference** | Where Japan surrendered on 14 August |
| **USS Missouri** | The ship in Tokyo Bay where the formal surrender documents were signed on 2 September |

# 8 The Holocaust, 1933–1945

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Definition

The Holocaust was the **systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six
million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and
collaborators**. It began in **1933** when Hitler came to power and ended in
**1945** when the Allies defeated the Axis. It is also known as **the Shoah**,
meaning *catastrophe*.

## The target

**Antisemitism** is prejudice against, or hatred of, Jewish people. It was an
old and widespread prejudice dating back to the **Middle Ages (500–1400)**, when
Christians blamed Jews for the death of Jesus. The Nazis then **blamed Jews for
Germany's defeat in the First World War (1914–1918)**, saw Jews as a **separate,
inferior and dangerous race**, and had aimed since the First World War for a
**pure Aryan race**.

The Nazi definition was **racial rather than religious**: it included people who
identified as Christians and people who did not practise Judaism at all.

> The guide's own wording of this definition is damaged, and reads as though the
> Nazis defined Jews *as* Christians. Its sense is that the racial definition
> reached people who were Christian or non-practising — which is why conversion
> offered no protection.

## Practices of persecution

As Germany annexed much of Europe and the USSR, Nazi influence produced
religious and ethnic persecution and execution across Europe. **Persecution** is
hostility and ill-treatment on the basis of beliefs or ethnicity.

- **1935 Nuremberg race laws** — outlawed Jewish–German marriages and stripped
  citizenship
- **Antisemitic propaganda**, boycotts of Jewish-owned businesses, and public
  humiliation through **badges** worn for identification
- **Violence** — for example **Kristallnacht**, concerted violence by Nazis
  against Jews throughout Germany and Austria
- **Ghettos, deportation and isolation**
- **Internment** — imprisoning people
- **Confiscation of Jewish property** and **forced labour**
- Prohibiting sexual relations between Jews and *German blooded people*

Hitler was the main leader, alongside Nazi leaders including **Hermann Göring,
Heinrich Himmler, Reinhard Heydrich and Adolf Eichmann**, other Axis powers, and
local institutions and bureaucracies.

## The Final Solution to the Jewish Question

Finalised at the **Wannsee Conference in January 1942**, the Final Solution was
the **deliberate and systematic mass murder of Jews** — the last stage of the
Holocaust, taking place from 1941 to 1945. **Liquidation** is the process of
dissolving ghetto administrative structures.

Two methods were used.

**1. Mass shooting**, on the outskirts of villages, towns and cities, on an
unprecedented scale and without shame: massacres were **conducted in daylight in
front of residents**. The German units involved included the **Einsatzgruppen**
(special task forces of the SS and police), Order Police battalions and Waffen-SS
units, with the German military providing logistical support.

**2. Gas poisoning**, at killing centres and with mobile gas vans using carbon
monoxide exhaust. This took the name **euthanasia** or *mercy death*, the Nazis
disguising mass murder by telling victims they were to be given showers.

### Killing centres

From late 1941 the Nazis built killing centres in German-occupied Poland, also
called **extermination camps** or **death camps**. Five operated: **Chelmno,
Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau**. They murdered Jews using
poisonous gas. The Nazis disguised their intentions when deporting Jews by
calling the deportations **resettlement actions**. Conditions were inhumane, and
some stronger Jews were sent to forced labour instead.

### Ghettos

**Ghettos** were areas of cities or towns where German occupiers forced Jews to
live in **overcrowded and unsanitary conditions**, enclosed by walls with guards
ensuring nobody escaped. Their purpose was as **holding sites prior to
deportation or murder**; the original purpose was to **isolate and control large
local Jewish populations** in occupied eastern Europe. The first were created in
German-occupied Poland, in **Warsaw and Lodz**.

Jews there were exploited through **forced labour in factories and workshops**,
with minimal food, extreme temperatures, and physical torture and attacks by
Nazis.

Jews in the ghettos **maintained a sense of dignity and community**, and
practised both spiritual and physical resistance: spiritually through the
**Shabbat archive**, and in **armed resistance** through the **Warsaw ghetto
uprising of 1943**.

## Who carried it out

The organisations were the **Nazi Party**, the **SA** (stormtroopers) and the
**SS** (*Schutzstaffel*, Protection Squadron). The German military, national
railway and healthcare systems, the German civil service and criminal justice
systems, and companies and banks all assisted with the Final Solution.

Some Germans cheered as Jews were beaten, and took their Jewish neighbours'
property. Other Axis powers and **Vichy France**, German-backed local
bureaucracies, and local police forces deported Jews. Some citizens denounced
Jews to German authorities and exposed their hiding places, then took their
valuables.

The motives given for German citizens are **enthusiasm, fear and self-interest**,
though **most individuals were bystanders**. Many helped because Nazi propaganda
reinforced longstanding local antisemitic prejudices; the *jew hunters* acted
either from ideological alignment with the Nazis or for **monetary rewards**.

## Other victims

The Nazis targeted other groups as threats to the health, unity and security of
the German people:

1. **Political opponents** — officials and members of other political parties,
   and those merely suspected of opposing the regime; sent to concentration camps
   or arrested if they refused military service
2. **Germans practising *dangerous activities*** — men accused of homosexuality,
   and *asocials* (beggars, prostitutes, alcoholics); also sent to concentration camps
3. **Black people**
4. **People with disabilities**
5. **Minorities** including Roma, Poles and Soviet prisoners of war
6. **Communists, Socialists and Jehovah's Witnesses**

## The end, and after

When the war ended, after the strategic and systematic bombing of Hitler's
occupied territories, he lost power and took his own life. The USSR and the
Americans **liberated surviving prisoners and survivors of death marches**.

But prejudice did not end with the war: some survivors, though physically alive,
**faced ongoing antisemitism and displacement** in their new lives.

### Survivors

Most Jews who survived within Germany did so through **help from others**, both
Jewish and non-Jewish, who found hiding places, procured **false papers**
protecting Christian identities, and provided food and supplies — and through
**luck**.

Most survivors overall were those who **emigrated from Germany** once they saw the
signs, escaping to the United States or Britain. This was very difficult, because
**no country wanted them** — antisemitism had spread beyond Germany's borders.

### Consequences

Survivors confronted the trauma of having lost entire families. Some had PTSD
from the war; some were isolated; deportations still occurred to a limited extent
in Hungary. Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators had **completely
devastated thousands of Jewish communities across Europe**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The Holocaust** | The systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi regime and its allies and collaborators |
| **The Shoah** | The other name for the Holocaust, meaning catastrophe |
| **Antisemitism** | Prejudice against or hatred of Jewish people |
| **Persecution** | Hostility and ill-treatment on the basis of beliefs or ethnicity |
| **Nuremberg race laws** | The 1935 laws outlawing Jewish–German marriages and removing citizenship |
| **Kristallnacht** | Concerted Nazi violence against Jews throughout Germany and Austria |
| **Internment** | Imprisoning people |
| **Wannsee Conference** | The January 1942 conference at which the Final Solution was finalised |
| **The Final Solution** | The deliberate and systematic mass murder of Jews, 1941–1945 |
| **Liquidation** | The process of dissolving ghetto administrative structures |
| **Einsatzgruppen** | Special task forces of the SS and police that carried out mass shootings |
| **Euthanasia** | The Nazi euphemism for gas poisoning, presented as mercy death |
| **Killing centres** | Extermination or death camps in German-occupied Poland: Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Auschwitz-Birkenau |
| **Resettlement actions** | The Nazi euphemism disguising deportations to killing centres |
| **Ghettos** | Walled areas where occupiers forced Jews to live in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions as holding sites before deportation or murder |
| **Warsaw ghetto uprising** | The 1943 armed resistance by Jews in the Warsaw ghetto |
| **SS** | The Schutzstaffel or Protection Squadron |
| **SA** | The Nazi stormtroopers |
